description: We’re a Sydney team of four (Andre, Johanna, David and Shaf) who took on Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data. We built Seed Data, a web app that helps Australian grain farmers choose a crop rotation for their paddock. It turns ten years of NASA POWER weather and MODIS greenness data into a short story about any paddock, then ranks rotations for the farmer’s goals. Every number has a source. Try it: https://seed-data-nasa.vercel.app
summary:
Seed Data helps Australian grain farmers answer one question as the seasons shift: which crop rotation suits my paddock now?

A farmer or agronomist picks one of twelve pilot paddocks across Australia's grain belt, or taps any spot on the map to fetch ten years of NASA POWER data live. Seed Data tells that paddock's decade as a short story with charts: growing-season rain and how much it varies, frost at flowering, heat at grain fill, and months of bare ground from MODIS greenness.

The farmer then sets what matters to them (saving water, improving soil, reducing risk, extra income), and Seed Data ranks three rotations, including the one they grow now, using transparent, published rules. Every score and sentence is built from numbered facts with a source and period. An optional AI narrator can reword the story, compare two paddocks or answer questions, but a checker rejects any number that isn't one of those facts.

Seed Data turns free NASA records into evidence a farmer and their agronomist can check, and it says plainly what the data can't tell them.
details:
Live app: https://seed-data-nasa.vercel.app
Code (public): https://github.com/davidnguyen65536/SeedData
Demo video (30 s): https://youtu.be/kVB4XNWzDsM
Interactive deck: https://seed-data-nasa.vercel.app/deck
Slide deck (PDF): https://github.com/davidnguyen65536/SeedData/blob/main/app/deck/SeedData_slides.pdf
Scoring rules: https://github.com/davidnguyen65536/SeedData/blob/main/docs/methodology.md

What it does. SeedData is a web app that helps Australian dryland grain farmers and their agronomists choose a crop rotation for one paddock, using ten years (2016–2025) of NASA Earth observations. Five tabs follow one question in order:

  1. Paddock: pick one of twelve pilot paddocks in NSW, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia and Queensland, or tap anywhere on the map to analyse that spot with NASA POWER data fetched live.
  2. Story: the paddock’s decade in five chapters with year-by-year charts, read-aloud, a side-by-side comparison with another paddock, and questions answered only from the paddock’s facts, each answer shown with a matching chart.
  3. Options: set how much each goal matters (saving water, improving soil, reducing risk, extra income), whether you run livestock and what you grow now. Three rotations are ranked: what you grow now, a legume break (field pea) and a pasture phase (lucerne), each scored 0–5 per goal with things to check locally and “Why this score?” in plain English.
  4. Data: every number grouped by source with its period, and what the data can’t tell you.
  5. How it works: the method, the team and a plain-language glossary.

How it works. Python pipelines download NASA POWER daily weather and soil wetness and MODIS NDVI greenness for each paddock and turn them into features: growing-season rain (April–October) and its year-to-year variation, the driest season, frost days at flowering (August–October), hot days at grain fill (October–November), heavy-rain days, topsoil wetness at sowing and months of bare ground. Published rules score each rotation 0–5 per goal, weighted by the farmer’s choices. Each result becomes numbered facts with source and period; fixed rules or, optionally, an AI model write the wording, and a deterministic checker rejects any number that isn’t one of the facts.

Benefits and intended impact.

  • A farmer sees what the last ten years actually looked like on their paddock, and the trade-offs of changing rotation, before committing a season to it.
  • Every number traces to a NASA dataset and period, so an agronomist can check it, challenge it and build advice on it.
  • It works for any spot in Australia with no login, because NASA POWER is fetched live.
  • It is open about uncertainty: it lists data gaps and local checks, and the AI can never invent a figure.

How it is creative. It tells a paddock’s climate as a story, not a dashboard of numbers, with an optional narrator in four voices (farmer, general public, judges, storyteller) that can read it aloud. The AI is fenced in: it may choose words, never numbers. Tapping anywhere on the map turns any farm into a scored paddock in seconds. The front page is a live farm drawn in text characters.

What we considered.

  • Trust: farmers act on advice they can check, so every figure shows its source and period, and the rules are published.
  • Australian coverage: many challenge datasets (SSURGO, CropScape, PRISM, OpenET) are US-only, so we chose NASA POWER and MODIS, which cover Australia.
  • Scale and uncertainty: NASA POWER cells are about 50 km and MODIS pixels 250 m, so results are indicative and the app says so.
  • Regional differences: frost and heat windows suit southern winter cropping; northern paddocks such as Moree and Dalby are flagged to check locally.
  • Access: plain words with a glossary, screen-reader descriptions for every chart, works on phones, and runs without an AI key.

Tools and languages. Python (pandas, NumPy, requests, pytest) for pipelines; JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the web app; Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for the map; Three.js for the front page; NASA POWER API and the ORNL DAAC MODIS web service; Claude (Anthropic) via a serverless function for optional wording; hosted on Vercel.

AI use: code and documentation were drafted with Claude (Anthropic) from the team’s design and reviewed and tested by the team. Details: https://github.com/davidnguyen65536/SeedData/blob/main/docs/si-disclosure.md
